messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 40
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Software Engineer
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 37

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Positive Reframing: I force myself to think only positive thoughts, Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Threat: Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Omar is a 40-year-old software engineer who lives with his wife and two children in a suburban development outside of Houston. He came to therapy at his wife’s insistence, six months after Hurricane Harvey flooded his neighborhood and nearly killed his family. Omar had been working from home that afternoon when the bayou behind his house began to rise. By the time he realized the water was not stopping, it was already seeping under the front door. He grabbed his children, ages five and seven, and his wife, and they climbed into the attic as the water rose to chest height in the living room. In the attic, the sound of the water rushing against the walls was deafening, a low roar punctuated by the crash of furniture slamming into walls below them. His youngest daughter was screaming, and Omar remembers only fragments: the darkness, the smell of wet insulation, his wife’s voice saying “we’re going to be okay” over and over, and then the sound of the Coast Guard helicopter blades, which seemed to come from everywhere and nowhere at once. He cannot put the sequence in order. The memories come back as a single, overwhelming moment: the roar, the smell, the terror, all at once, as if he is back in that attic. Sometimes, when he is trying to fall asleep, he hears the water again, clear as day.

In the months since, Omar has come to believe that he should have prevented the situation entirely. He tells himself that somebody else—somebody more prepared, more competent—would not have gotten his family into that kind of danger. He had lived in that house for twelve years; he knew the bayou flooded. Why had he not left earlier? Why had he not moved them to a hotel when the first warnings came? He used to be a happy person, joking with his coworkers, coaching his son’s soccer team. Now he feels hollow, convinced that nothing good can happen to him anymore. He has stopped answering calls from friends. He stopped coaching. When his wife suggests they take the kids to the lake for the weekend, he feels a wave of dread and says no, without explanation.

The world has become a landscape of potential threats. When someone at the grocery store steps into his peripheral vision unexpectedly, Omar’s entire body lurches, his heart hammering, before he can even register what happened. If his wife touches his shoulder from behind while he is working at his computer, he flinches away, sometimes shouting before he can stop himself. He has started scanning every room he enters for exits. At his office, he sits with his back to the wall so he can see the door and the stairwell. He cannot explain why this feels necessary—he is not in a war zone, he is in a cubicle—but the feeling is absolute: if he does not know the way out, he is trapped.

Omar has also developed a deep aversion to medical settings. When his daughter needed a routine checkup, he told his wife he had a deadline and could not come. The truth was that the sight of the ambulance bay at the clinic, the smell of antiseptic, the sound of a gurney being wheeled down a hall—all of it brought him back to the attic, to the moment he thought they would not make it. He forces himself to think only positive thoughts when these feelings arise, repeating “we are safe, we are fine” under his breath, but the relief never lasts. He also finds himself, late at night, replaying the storm in his mind, but not the helpless parts. Instead, he imagines himself doing something violent to the storm itself, or to the water, or to the man on the news who said the levees would hold. He ruminates about getting even, though he knows there is no one to get even with.

What finally brought Omar to seek help was a moment at his son’s school. A fire drill sounded, and Omar, who had come to pick up his son early, dropped to his knees in the hallway, shaking, unable to breathe. A teacher helped him to a chair, and he heard himself say, “I thought it was the water.” That night, his wife told him she was afraid for him, and for their children, and he saw the look on her face—the same look she had in the attic. He agreed to come to therapy because he does not want to lose his family a second time, even though he is not sure what good talking can do. What frightens him most is the thought that this is just who he is now, that the happy person he used to be is gone for good.
